title: Pets.com, the sock puppet company, goes public
what: Pets.com of San Francisco sold 7.5 million shares on the Nasdaq on February 11, raising $82.5 million at a price that valued the company at about $325 million. It sells pet food and supplies online and is famous for its sock-puppet mascot, which appeared in a Super Bowl advertisement in January. In its first year, to December 1999, it had sales of $5.8 million and a net loss of $61.8 million; Amazon.com owns about 30% of it. Amazon, the other early investors and the managers have agreed not to sell until August, and some of them longer.
why: The listing beat (importance 1). The case for buying was the brand, the Amazon connection and a huge pet-supplies market; the case against was in the prospectus: it sold heavy, low-margin goods below cost and spent heavily on advertising. The shares closed the month at 7, already below the issue price.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/000089161800000749/0000891618-00-000749.txt (IPO prospectus, 424B4 of February 11, 2000, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pets.com (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/0000891618-00-000749.txt (same prospectus, 'Shares Eligible for Future Sale': 180-day lock-up agreements; 13,420,045 shares eligible 180 days after the prospectus of 10 February 2000, further blocks to January 2001; read 2026-10-17)
changed: lock-up rule: only the month the lock-up ends, no share counts or durations

title: Pets.com loses 39% as investors count the dot-coms' cash
what: Pets.com's prospectus shows how fast the money goes: in the last three months of 1999 it sold pet supplies for $5.2 million, paid more for the goods and shipping than customers paid for them, and lost $42.4 million. It had $30.2 million in cash at the end of the year and about $76 million more from its February share sale, which the company says is enough for at least twelve months; at the fourth quarter's pace that money covers only about two and a half quarters of losses. On March 20 the financial weekly Barron's warned in a cover story that at least 51 of 207 internet companies it studied will run out of cash within twelve months. Pets.com shares fell 39% in March, while the S&P 500 rose 10%.
why: The question that killed Pets.com: -39% in March 2000, a month after the IPO, while the market rose. The Barron's cash-burn study of 20 March is the context; whether Pets.com was on its list is unknown (the full table is not reproduced online).
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/0000891618-00-000749.txt (Pets.com prospectus, 424B4 of 11 February 2000: summary financial data, liquidity) (read 2026-10-17); https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/articles/cashburn.htm (Jack Willoughby, 'Burning Up', Barron's, 20 March 2000) (read 2026-10-17); data/out/pets-com.json and data/reference/sp500.json (March 2000 changes) (read 2026-10-17)
changed: note to the writer addressed: the story is now about Pets.com (its fourth-quarter 1999 loss, its cash after the IPO, its 39% fall against a rising S&P 500), with Barron's cash warning for internet companies as the context and no crash; Pets.com is not named in the reproduced Barron's text and its place in the full table could not be found, and no 10-K for 1999 is on EDGAR, so the figures come from the February prospectus

title: Pets.com sells at a loss
what: Pets.com reported sales of $7.7 million for the first quarter, against $12.5 million spent on the goods and shipping, and $28.9 million on marketing. The net loss was $39.1 million. The company said its gross margin improved from minus 124% to minus 64% after it opened a second warehouse in Indianapolis.
why: The numbers behind the legend: every sale lost money even before advertising. -27% in May 2000.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/000089161800002857/0000891618-00-002857.txt (10-Q for the quarter to March 31, 2000, filed May 15, 2000, read 2026-10-03)

title: Pets.com says its cash will last only into early 2001
what: In its quarterly report filed on August 14 Pets.com said its cash should be enough only into the first quarter of 2001 and that it expects to have to raise more money then. It is still selling goods for less than they cost. And on 8 August the lock-up from the public offering ended: Amazon, the other early investors and the managers may now sell. In August the shares fell 40%, while the stock market rose 6%.
why: With investors no longer funding loss-making dot-coms, this was close to a death notice: -40% in August.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/000089161800004394/e10-q.txt (10-Q for the quarter to June 30, 2000, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pets.com (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/0000891618-00-000749.txt (IPO prospectus: 13,420,045 shares, 45.4%, eligible 180 days after the prospectus of 10 February 2000, i.e. 8 August 2000; read 2026-10-17)
changed: end of the lock-up on 8 August 2000 added (curator's wish, research note lockups.md); move kept; lock-up rule: only the month the lock-up ends, no share counts or durations

title: Pets.com cuts costs and looks for a buyer
what: Pets.com opened a customer service centre in Greenwood, Indiana, and moved most of its customer staff there to cut costs. It is trying to raise capital or sell the company.
why: The last attempts at rescue; -23% in September.

title: Pets.com shuts down
what: On November 7 Pets.com said it will stop taking orders on November 9, lay off 255 of its 320 employees and sell its inventory, warehouse equipment, web addresses and the sock-puppet brand. More than 50 possible buyers and investors were approached; none would fund or buy the company. The shares, issued at $11 in February, traded at about 19 cents, and the company warned that shareholders may receive little or nothing.
why: The exit (importance 1): liquidated nine months after its IPO, the symbol of dot-com folly. In December the company estimated shareholders might eventually receive up to about 25 cents a share; the game ends the position at the November price.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/0001095811-00-004383.txt (8-K with press release, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pets.com (read 2026-10-03); liquidation estimate from https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/000109581100005560/f67985dsdefs14a.txt (read 2026-10-03)
